summary.text: For every prime \(p\), the only admissible integers at most \(p\) are \(1\) and \(p\), so \(a(p)\le 2\). Taking \(\epsilon=\tfrac12\), arbitrarily large primes have \(\sqrt{\log p}>2\), contradicting the asserted eventual lower bound along the primes.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\#\{k\in\mathbb N:1\le k\le n\text{ and every prime factor of }k\text{ is also a prime factor of }n\}.
\]
We prove that the asserted eventual lower bound is false.

The key observation is that the values of \(a(n)\) remain bounded when \(n\) ranges over the primes. Specifically, if \(p\) is prime, then
\[
a(p)\le 2.
\]
Indeed, the set of prime factors of \(p\) is the singleton \(\{p\}\). Consider an integer \(k\) counted by \(a(p)\). Thus \(1\le k\le p\), and every prime factor of \(k\) lies in \(\{p\}\). If \(k=1\), this gives one possible value. If \(k>1\), then \(k\) has at least one prime divisor; choose such a divisor \(q\). By the prime-factor condition, \(q=p\). Consequently \(p\mid k\), and in particular \(p\le k\). Since already \(k\le p\), it follows that \(k=p\). Hence every integer counted by \(a(p)\) belongs to \(\{1,p\}\), proving \(a(p)\le2\). (In fact both values are counted, so \(a(p)=2\), but the upper bound is all that is needed.)

Now specialize the proposed statement to
\[
\epsilon=\frac12>0.
\]
If the conjecture were true, there would be some \(N\in\mathbb N\) such that for every integer \(n\ge N\),
\[
(\log n)^{1-1/2}=(\log n)^{1/2}\le a(n).
\tag{1}
\]

On the other hand,
\[
(\log x)^{1/2}\longrightarrow +\infty\qquad (x\longrightarrow+\infty).
\]
This follows because \(\log x\to+\infty\), and raising a positive quantity to the positive power \(1/2\) also tends to infinity. Therefore there exists a real number \(M\) such that
\[
x\ge M\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 2<(\log x)^{1/2}.
\tag{2}
\]

There are arbitrarily large primes. Choose a natural number \(m\) with \(m\ge M\), and then choose a prime \(p\ge\max\{N,m\}\). Thus \(p\ge N\) and, viewing \(p\) as a real number, \(p\ge M\).

Because \(p\ge N\), equation (1) applied to \(n=p\) gives
\[
(\log p)^{1/2}\le a(p).
\]
Because \(p\) is prime, the preceding classification gives \(a(p)\le2\). Hence
\[
(\log p)^{1/2}\le2.
\tag{3}
\]
But \(p\ge M\), so (2) gives
\[
2<(\log p)^{1/2},
\tag{4}
\]
contradicting (3).

Thus the claimed assertion
\[
\forall\epsilon>0\;\exists N\;\forall n\ge N,
\qquad a(n)\ge(\log n)^{1-\epsilon}
\]
is false. The obstruction is the infinite subsequence of prime arguments: along every prime \(p\), the value is only \(a(p)=2\), whereas for \(\epsilon=\tfrac12\) the proposed lower bound \((\log p)^{1/2}\) grows without bound.
